content: payments-service is owned by the payments-platform team; PagerDuty escalation policy is payments-platform-primary, secondary rotation payments-platform-secondary.
payments-service exposes POST /v1/charges, which requires an Idempotency-Key header; requests without one are rejected with 400 before touching the acquirer.
payments-service exposes POST /v1/refunds, which is only callable by orders-api and the internal support console, gated by a service-to-service JWT issued by auth-gateway.
payments-service p99 latency SLO is 250ms, measured at the internal ALB target group, excluding acquirer round-trip time which is tracked separately.
payments-service persists charge and refund records to the legacy payments table in the aurora-payments-pg cluster.

payments-service now persists charge and refund records to payments_v2, not the legacy payments table. The 2026-06 schema migration split settlement fields into payments_v2 for the multi-currency rollout; the legacy payments table is read-only and kept for reconciliation queries only.
payments-service publishes to the payment.events Kafka topic (12 partitions, key = charge_id) after a successful capture or refund; ledger-worker is the sole consumer group.
payments-service calls acquirer-gateway (the Vantage Acquiring integration) synchronously over HTTPS for authorize and capture; this is the single hardest external dependency in the charge path.
payments-service depends on aurora-payments-pg for all reads and writes in the charge path; there is no local cache in front of it for charge state.

payments-service runs pgbouncer in transaction-pooling mode with max_client_conn 40 per pod against aurora-payments-pg; raising this without also raising Aurora max_connections has caused connection storms before.
The acquirer-gateway client in payments-service opens its circuit breaker after 5 consecutive 5xx responses within a 30s window, and half-opens for a single probe request after 60s.
payments-service is rate limited at 500 req/s per API key; the limit is enforced by auth-gateway before the request reaches payments-service, not by payments-service itself.

Failover runbook (v1): on a payments-service failover, restart ledger-worker before payments-service so the ledger consumer resumes first and drains any in-flight ledger writes before payments-service starts accepting traffic again.

Failover runbook v2 (supersedes v1): restart payments-service before ledger-worker during a failover. The v1 order (ledger-worker first) is what caused INC-4471 -- ledger-worker replayed in-flight events against a payments-service instance whose Aurora connection pool had not yet re-established, producing 143 duplicate charge attempts. Always restart payments-service first now.
payments-service runs in us-east-1 only; there is no active-active multi-region deployment yet, which is a known gap tracked as a postmortem action item from INC-4519.

During INC-4471 (2026-05-12, SEV2), payments-service began returning 503s after an on-call engineer followed runbook:payments-failover v1 and restarted ledger-worker before payments-service. Replayed in-flight ledger events hit a payments-service instance that had not yet re-established its Aurora connection pool, producing 143 duplicate charge attempts before priya manually paused the ledger-worker consumer group.

priya resolved INC-4471 by manually pausing the ledger-worker-cg consumer group via kafka-consumer-groups --reset-offsets was avoided in favor of a plain pause, restarting payments-service, confirming Aurora pool health, then resuming ledger-worker. Action item: rewrite runbook:payments-failover with the corrected restart order.

INC-4560 (2026-07-03, SEV3): acquirer-gateway p99 response time rose to 2.1s for roughly 20 minutes; payments-service's circuit breaker opened correctly after 5 consecutive 5xx, shedding load onto the retry queue instead of cascading. No customer-visible failures; closed as acquirer-side.

INC-4519 (2026-05-30, SEV1): an AWS us-east-1a AZ network event took out one of payments-service's three pod replicas plus the aurora-payments-pg writer's AZ, forcing an Aurora failover that took 34 seconds; payments-service saw a 34-second full outage on writes. Action item: evaluate multi-region for the charge path.

INC-4538 (2026-06-20, SEV3): orders-api briefly reused an Idempotency-Key across two distinct checkout attempts due to a client-side retry bug, causing payments-service to correctly reject the second charge as a duplicate. No money moved incorrectly; flagged as a false alarm after devon traced it to orders-api's retry logic, not payments-service.

Current investigation (task 2026-08-03-oncall): correlating a payments-service p99 latency spike (640ms vs the 250ms SLO) with elevated CPU on the aurora-payments-pg primary; ledger-worker consumer lag on payment.events is climbing (18k messages, was under 500 an hour ago). Next step: check for a long-running migration or autovacuum on aurora-payments-pg before paging payments-platform secondary.
orders-api is owned by the checkout-experience team; PagerDuty escalation policy checkout-experience-primary.

orders-api exposes POST /v1/orders, which synchronously calls payments-service POST /v1/charges before confirming the order; if payments-service does not respond within 3s, orders-api falls back to degraded mode.
orders-api persists orders to orders_v2 in the aurora-payments-pg cluster (orders schema); order state transitions are appended, never overwritten in place.

orders-api depends on payments-service synchronously for charge authorization at checkout time; a payments-service outage puts orders-api into degraded mode (orders held as pending_payment rather than rejected outright).
orders-api validates every incoming customer session token against auth-gateway before creating an order; token validation is cached for 60s to reduce load on redis-session.
orders-api publishes to the order.events Kafka topic (8 partitions, key = order_id) on every order state transition; ledger-worker and notification-fanout both consume it.

orders-api retries a failed payments-service charge call up to 3 times with exponential backoff (200ms, 800ms, 3200ms) and always reuses the same Idempotency-Key across retries, per the 2026-06 fix for INC-4538.
orders-api's end-to-end p99 latency SLO for POST /v1/orders is 400ms, which includes the synchronous call into payments-service.
orders-api rate limits order creation to 200 req/s per seller account, backed by counters in redis-ratelimit with a 1s sliding window.

devon traced INC-4538 to an orders-api client that generated a new Idempotency-Key on retry instead of reusing the original one from the first attempt, which is what let a legitimate retry look like a duplicate charge to payments-service. Fixed 2026-06-20 by pinning the key at request-construction time.

During INC-4519, orders-api correctly entered degraded mode when payments-service dropped writes for 34 seconds; 212 orders were held as pending_payment and successfully reconciled automatically once payments-service recovered. No manual intervention needed on the orders-api side.

INC-4650 (2026-07-22, SEV3): a bad feature flag rollout (checkout-experience.new-tax-calc at 100%) caused a 12% error rate on POST /v1/orders due to a null-pointer on international addresses; rolled back the flag within 9 minutes of the alert firing.

Current investigation (task 2026-08-03-oncall): orders-api's degraded-mode entry rate has been elevated (4.2% of requests vs a normal baseline under 0.5%) for the last 20 minutes, tracking the same window as the payments-service latency spike being investigated separately. Hypothesis: shared root cause on aurora-payments-pg, not two independent incidents.
ledger-worker is owned by the payments-platform team, same on-call rotation as payments-service.
ledger-worker consumes payment.events under consumer group ledger-worker-cg and writes double-entry rows to ledger_entries for every capture and refund.
ledger-worker also consumes order.events under the same ledger-worker-cg consumer group to record order-cancellation reversal entries in the ledger.
ledger-worker is the only writer to the ledger_entries table in aurora-payments-pg; every write is a double-entry pair (debit + credit) inserted in the same transaction.
ledger-worker publishes to ledger.events after committing a ledger entry; this feeds the downstream reconciliation and finance reporting pipeline, which is out of scope for on-call.

ledger-worker deduplicates replayed Kafka messages using a unique constraint on (charge_id, event_type) in ledger_entries; a replay of an already-applied event is a no-op insert conflict, not a duplicate ledger row. This is the guard that was missing context in the runbook:payments-failover v1 restart order, though the constraint itself did not fail during INC-4471 -- the duplicate charges happened upstream in payments-service, not in the ledger.
ledger-worker's consumer lag alert on payment.events and order.events fires at 5000 messages behind, which at normal throughput represents roughly 6 minutes of backlog.

ledger-worker commits Kafka offsets only after the ledger_entries insert transaction commits, so a restart resumes exactly where it left off with no data loss and no gap -- the risk in INC-4471 was ordering relative to payments-service, not ledger-worker's own restart safety.

During INC-4471, ledger-worker-cg was paused for 41 of the 47 incident minutes while priya restarted payments-service in the correct order; no ledger_entries were lost because offsets had not yet been committed for the in-flight batch.

INC-4590 (2026-06-28, SEV3): ledger-worker consumer lag on payment.events crossed 5000 messages after a missing index on ledger_entries(charge_id) made the dedup uniqueness check do a sequential scan under load; adding the index dropped write latency from 180ms to 4ms per insert.

Current investigation (task 2026-08-03-oncall): ledger-worker consumer lag on payment.events is at 18k and climbing (started at under 500), which lines up with the aurora-payments-pg CPU spike also being investigated on payments-service. No alert on ledger_entries insert latency yet, so leaning toward payments-service or the Aurora primary as the shared root cause rather than ledger-worker itself.
auth-gateway is owned by the identity-platform team; PagerDuty escalation policy identity-platform-primary.
auth-gateway stores active session tokens and a refresh-token revocation list in redis-session; a full redis-session flush would force every logged-in user to re-authenticate.
auth-gateway issues customer session JWTs with a 900-second (15 minute) expiry; refresh tokens are valid for 30 days and are checked against the redis-session revocation list on every use.

auth-gateway enforces the 500 req/s per API key limit on behalf of payments-service, using counters in redis-ratelimit with a 1-second sliding window, rejecting over-limit requests with 429 before they reach payments-service.
auth-gateway depends on redis-session for every token validation call; there is no local fallback cache, so a redis-session outage is a full auth outage across every downstream service.

auth-gateway rotates its JWT signing key every 90 days, publishing the new public key to the JWKS endpoint 24 hours before the old key is retired to give downstream services time to refresh their cached key set.

INC-4501 (2026-05-08, SEV2): a manual key rotation skipped the 24-hour JWKS overlap window, so auth-gateway started signing with the new key before orders-api and payments-service had refreshed their cached JWKS, causing a 6-minute spike in 401s across checkout. Fixed by automating the rotation script to enforce the overlap.

On 2026-06-02, redis-session's ElastiCache primary failed over to its replica after a node-level hardware fault; auth-gateway saw a 4-second connection blip with no auth outage because the client library retried against the new primary automatically. Logged for visibility, not a paged incident.

Checked as part of task 2026-08-03-oncall: auth-gateway latency and error rate are both nominal; redis-session and redis-ratelimit are healthy. Ruled out as a contributor to the current payments-service / orders-api investigation.
notification-fanout is owned by the checkout-experience team, on the same rotation as orders-api.
notification-fanout consumes order.events to send order-confirmation and shipping-update emails and webhooks to sellers.
notification-fanout also consumes payment.events to send receipt emails to buyers after a successful capture.
notification-fanout routes any notification that fails delivery after 5 attempts to the notification.dlq topic; a background job replays the DLQ every 6 hours after backoff.
notification-fanout uses redis-ratelimit to throttle notifications per recipient to at most 1 email per 10 seconds and 1 SMS per 60 seconds, to avoid flooding a seller during a burst of order events.
notification-fanout runs under consumer group notification-fanout-cg with 8 partitions matching order.events; it is horizontally scaled to one consumer per partition.

INC-4530 (2026-06-11, SEV3): the external email provider had a 40-minute outage; notification-fanout correctly backed off and queued to notification.dlq rather than crashing, and the DLQ replay job cleared the backlog within 15 minutes of the provider recovering. No message loss.

As a side effect of INC-4650 (the checkout-experience.new-tax-calc rollback), some orders that briefly failed and were retried by orders-api generated two order-confirmation emails via notification-fanout before the redis-ratelimit throttle caught the second one. Considered low severity; not a paged item on its own.
Checked as part of task 2026-08-03-oncall: notification-fanout consumer lag is normal and notification.dlq depth is at baseline. Ruled out as a contributor.
aurora-payments-pg runs as 1 writer instance plus 2 reader replicas in us-east-1, hosting the payments, payments_v2, orders_v2, and ledger_entries tables across separate schemas.
aurora-payments-pg's writer instance is a db.r6g.2xlarge; the last capacity review (2026-04) concluded this has headroom to roughly 3x current peak write throughput before a resize is needed.
aurora-payments-pg has continuous backups enabled with point-in-time recovery and a 35-day retention window; a manual snapshot is also taken before every schema migration.

aurora-payments-pg's max_connections is set to 2000; combined pgbouncer pools across payments-service, orders-api, and ledger-worker are budgeted to stay under 1200 to leave headroom for migrations and ad-hoc queries.

aurora-payments-pg has an index ledger_entries_charge_id_idx on ledger_entries(charge_id) added 2026-06-28 after INC-4590; before that, the dedup uniqueness check on ledger_entries was a sequential scan under load.

During INC-4519, aurora-payments-pg's writer failed over to a reader after the us-east-1a AZ network event; the failover itself took 34 seconds, matching the payments-service write outage duration exactly, confirming the Aurora failover was the root cause rather than an application bug.

Current investigation (task 2026-08-03-oncall): the aurora-payments-pg writer's CPU is at 91% (baseline is 35-45%), and pg_stat_activity shows a long-running ANALYZE on payments_v2 that started 25 minutes ago and has not completed; suspected cause of the downstream payments-service and ledger-worker symptoms. Next step: confirm with marcus before killing the ANALYZE.
kafka-payments is a 3-broker Amazon MSK cluster in us-east-1 hosting order.events, payment.events, ledger.events, and notification.dlq; replication factor is 3 on every production topic.
kafka-payments retains messages for 168 hours (7 days) on all topics, which is what makes it safe to fully replay ledger-worker's consumer group from the start of a bad deploy window if needed.
kafka-payments topics are configured with min.insync.replicas=2, so a single broker failure does not block producers, but a two-broker failure would.

On 2026-07-15, MSK performed a routine broker replacement on kafka-payments broker 2; no producer or consumer impact was observed because min.insync.replicas=2 covered the single-broker gap. Logged as an FYI, not an incident.

Checked as part of task 2026-08-03-oncall: kafka-payments broker health, ISR counts, and under-replicated-partitions are all nominal. The consumer lag being seen on ledger-worker is downstream of Aurora, not a broker-side problem.
redis-session is an ElastiCache Redis cluster (cluster-mode disabled, primary + 1 replica) dedicated to auth-gateway's session and refresh-token revocation data.
redis-session sets a TTL of 900 seconds on session tokens, matching auth-gateway's access-token expiry; refresh-token revocation entries are set with a 30-day TTL instead.
redis-session uses the volatile-ttl eviction policy, so if memory pressure ever forces eviction it drops the entries closest to expiring first rather than the least-recently-used ones.

On 2026-06-02, redis-session's ElastiCache primary node had a hardware fault and failed over to its replica automatically; total blip was 4 seconds and did not trigger a page (see the linked auth-gateway note in slack:#sre-oncall).
redis-ratelimit is a separate ElastiCache Redis cluster (cluster-mode enabled, 3 shards) dedicated to sliding-window rate-limit counters for auth-gateway, orders-api, and notification-fanout.

redis-ratelimit keys are namespaced per limiter and set with a TTL equal to the window size (1s for API-key limits, 10s for email throttling, 60s for SMS throttling), so stale counters self-clean without a sweep job.

On 2026-05-20, a routine redis-ratelimit shard rebalance caused a brief (under 2s) latency bump on rate-limit checks; auth-gateway's fail-open-on-timeout behavior meant a handful of requests briefly bypassed the limiter rather than being incorrectly rejected. Logged, not paged.
Checked as part of task 2026-08-03-oncall: redis-ratelimit shard health and latency are nominal. Ruled out as a contributor to the current investigation.
The current payments-platform secondary on-call is marcus for the week of 2026-07-28 through 2026-08-04; primary is priya.
The current checkout-experience secondary on-call is devon for the week of 2026-07-28 through 2026-08-04.

Tracked as an open action item from INC-4519: payments-service and aurora-payments-pg have no active-active multi-region failover; a full AZ or region loss in us-east-1 remains a hard outage bounded only by Aurora's single-region failover time.

ledger-worker has no dead-letter queue of its own; a message that repeatedly fails to insert (e.g. a constraint violation that is not the expected dedup conflict) will block the partition until an engineer manually intervenes. Tracked as a backlog item, not yet scheduled.

INC-4610 (2026-08-03, SEV2, in progress): paged at 14:12 UTC on payments-service p99 latency breaching SLO; orders-api degraded-mode rate and ledger-worker consumer lag both correlate with the same window. Incident channel slack:#incident-4610 opened; priya is IC.

Working hypothesis for INC-4610 (task 2026-08-03-oncall): the long-running ANALYZE on payments_v2 on the aurora-payments-pg writer is holding enough I/O and lock contention to slow down payments-service's write path, which cascades into orders-api degraded mode and ledger-worker consumer lag. Not yet confirmed; marcus is checking whether the ANALYZE was scheduled or ad-hoc.

notification-fanout has a single SMS provider integration with no automatic failover to a second provider; an SMS-provider outage falls back to email-only notification, which is acceptable for now per checkout-experience but is a known single point of failure.

orders-api's 60-second local cache of token validation results means a revoked token can remain accepted by orders-api for up to 60 seconds after auth-gateway revokes it; considered an acceptable tradeoff for latency, documented explicitly so it is never mistaken for a bug during an incident review.

INC-4650 was resolved by rolling back the checkout-experience.new-tax-calc flag to 0%; postmortem action items were to add an international-address test fixture to the flag's canary suite and require a 5% canary stage before any checkout-path flag goes to 100%.

Since INC-4650, any checkout-path feature flag in orders-api must go through a 5% canary stage for at least 30 minutes before advancing to 100%; this policy is enforced by the flag-rollout tooling, not just documentation.
INC-4590 was resolved by adding ledger_entries_charge_id_idx during a low-traffic window (02:00 UTC); consumer lag drained from 6200 messages to zero within 11 minutes of the index build completing.

payments-service supports USD, EUR, GBP, and CAD as of the 2026-06 multi-currency migration to payments_v2; currency conversion for display purposes happens in orders-api, not payments-service, which always stores and settles in the original charge currency.

The payments_v2 cutover on 2026-06-14 ran a 20-minute read-only maintenance window on the legacy payments table while a backfill job copied the trailing 48 hours of rows; orders-api served pending_payment for all checkouts during the window, exactly as designed by the degraded-mode fallback. Zero data loss confirmed by row-count reconciliation.

aurora-payments-pg uses one schema per owning service (payments, orders, ledger) even though all three currently share the same physical cluster; this was a deliberate choice to allow splitting into separate clusters later without a table-name collision.

the ledger.events topic on kafka-payments has 6 partitions, fewer than payment.events (12) or order.events (8), because its only consumers are the low-volume reconciliation and finance-reporting pipelines.

INC-4501's action item -- automating the JWKS overlap window in the key-rotation script -- shipped 2026-05-15; the next scheduled rotation (2026-08-13, per the 90-day cadence) will be the first fully automated one.
notification-fanout's p99 latency SLO is a comparatively loose 5000ms since notifications are async and best-effort relative to the synchronous checkout path.

Next step for INC-4610 (task 2026-08-03-oncall): waiting on marcus to confirm whether the long-running ANALYZE on payments_v2 was an ad-hoc query or the nightly scheduled job that ran late; if ad-hoc, kill it and page whoever ran it; if scheduled, consider moving the job window earlier to avoid overlap with EU morning traffic.
